bib.title: JARVIS-1: Open-World Multi-task Agents with Memory-Augmented Multimodal Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: JARVIS-1: Open-world Multi-task Agents with Memory-Augmented Multimodal Language Models. Zihao Wang, Shaofei Cai, Anji Liu, Yonggang Jin, Jinbing Hou, Bowei Zhang, Haowei Lin, Zhaofeng He, Zilong Zheng, Yaodong Yang, Xiaojian Ma, Yitao Liang (Team CraftJarvis). arXiv:2311.05997v3, 30 Nov 2023 (preprint).

COVERAGE: All 28 of 28 pages read, about 90,400 of 92,920 chars. I skipped roughly 2,500 chars in the middle of the reference list (offsets about 62,000 to 64,500). Appendices A to C and Tables 5 to 14 were read. Text extraction worked. Figure data (bar labels) came out as scrambled numbers, so I did not run the figure-caption script.

Relevance to the target note (03-memory-as-an-operating-system.md): the note's sources list does not contain this paper. JARVIS-1 is not about OS-style paging. It is an experience-memory / retrieval-augmented planning paper in Minecraft. If it is cited, it fits next to the Voyager / Generative Agents style memory entries, not next to MemGPT.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Memory-augmented planning roughly triples success on diamond tasks versus the same planner without memory (DEPS).
  number: 8.99% vs 2.42% (diamond group average)
  setup: Minecraft 1.16.5 survival, 11 task groups of 200+ tasks from the Minecraft Universe Benchmark, empty or iron_axe start, at least 30 seeds per task, GPT-based planner, memory filled over 4 epochs of self-instructed tasks before evaluation.
  quote: "In diamond-related tasks specifically, the success rate has increased by nearly 3 times (8.99% vs 2.42%)."
  where: p.11 (Table 2 on p.11)
- Memory cuts re-planning rounds.
  number: 2-3 rounds vs more than 6
  setup: same as above, compared with DEPS.
  quote: "JA RV I S-1 usually only requires 2-3 rounds of re-planning to generate the correct executable plan, whereas DEPS requires more than 6 rounds."
  where: p.11
- Success on ObtainDiamondPickaxe rises with game time and with memory growth, with no gradient update.
  number: 6.2% to 12.5% when time goes from 20 to 60 minutes; VPT-RL goes from 2.5% to 3%
  setup: 24,000 steps = 20 min, 72,000 steps = 60 min; agent trained 4 epochs on the full task pool; the task was evaluated over 300 times on different seeds (Fig 9 caption). Table 9 lists diamond_pickaxe at 0.0622 over 692 evals.
  quote: "JA RV I S-1’s success rate in acquiring a diamond pickaxe improved from 6.2% to 12.5%."
  where: p.14 (Fig 9)
- Reasoning before retrieval, then multimodal keys, beat text-only retrieval. Tested with three retrieval variants plus a no-memory baseline.
  number: none stated in text. The Fig 8 bar labels are scrambled in the extraction, so I cannot map them to variants. Read the figure before citing values.
  setup: subset of Minecraft tasks, all else held equal.
  quote: "The experiments show that reasoning before retrieval can effectively improve retrieval accuracy."
  where: p.13
- Memory size drives improvement. After 4 epochs of learning, memory held 425 successful trajectories.
  number: 425 trajectories
  setup: success rate by memory size on key tech-tree items (Fig 7).
  quote: "After 4 epochs of learning,JA RV I S-1 had accumulated a total of 425 successful trajectories in its memory."
  where: p.13 (Fig 7 caption)
- With memory, the weaker LM matches the stronger one. Open-source LLaMA2-70B lacks Minecraft knowledge. A fine-tuned LLaMA2-13B matches ChatGPT.
  number: none given in text
  setup: 4 epochs of learning, at least 20 seeds, task subset.
  quote: "ChatGPT, despite having fewer parameters, achieves nearly identical success rates as GPT-4. This suggests that language models equipped with memory can significantly enhance planning abilities."
  where: p.12 (Fig 6)
- The memory design is a key-value store. Keys are the task plus the observation. Values are the plans that were executed successfully. Only successes are stored.
  number: none
  quote: "it is a key-value memory where the keys are multimodal, comprising both the task and the observation (or situation) made when this memory entry was created. The values are the plans that were successfully executed."
  where: p.7; App A.3 p.23 ("memory is a list where each trajectory experience is encoded as a dictionary, including the keys task, state, and plan")
- Retrieval is two-stage. First, an LLM does backward-search query generation: it decomposes the task into depth-bounded sub-goals. Second, a CLIP text match filters candidates by a confidence threshold, then candidates are ranked by visual-state similarity. Only the top entry per sub-goal is retrieved.
  number: none
  quote: "We select the memory entries with similarity higher than the confidence threshold as the candidate entries. Then we will compute the visual state embedding of query and states in candidate entires."
  where: p.8 (Eq. 2, Fig 5)
- Self-instruct curriculum: the planner picks tasks from a pool. Parallel agents with a shared memory run them. Memory grows until it hits a capacity. A GPT-generated curriculum beat human-written and random curricula.
  number: none (comparison is in Fig 9)
  quote: "The results show thatJA RV I S-1 with a GPT-generated curriculum can finish the task within the shortest game-playing steps and achieve the best performance in 60 minutes."
  where: p.9 and p.14
- Self-check (simulate the plan's inventory before execution) and self-explain (use environment feedback to locate the bug and re-plan) form the interactive planner.
  number: none
  where: pp.6-7, Fig 4, prompts in App A.2
- Baseline comparison on the diamond pickaxe.
  number: 6.22% vs 2.5% within 20 min. The abstract claims 5x.
  quote: "JA RV I S-1 has more than doubled the success rate of obtaining a diamond pickaxe (6.22% vs 2.5% within 20 minutes)."
  where: p.14. Caveat: the abstract and conclusion say "5 times". The text supports about 2.5x at 20 min. Only the 60-minute figure (12.5%) is about 5x, and VPT is measured at 3% at 60 min, which would be about 4x.

LIMITS
- The authors concede the bottleneck is the controller, not the planner or memory: "the bottleneck for JARVIS-1 in tasks involving diamonds often lies with the Controller’s inability to perfectly execute short-horizon text instructions".
- Memory stores only successful trajectories. There is no eviction, summarization or forgetting, and no staleness handling. The memory grows until a "certain capacity".
- Evaluation is Minecraft only, in an easier setting: peaceful difficulty, permanent daytime, keepInventory, and night vision (App B.3).
- Baselines were reproduced by the authors from prompt and feedback templates (p.10). Human reference results are only for 10-minute play.
- The memory ablation numbers are only in figures. Memory "learning" happens before evaluation (4 epochs), so the benefit includes training-set exposure to the same task pool. Tasks within the same family help each other (Fig 2 right), so the transfer claim is confounded with overlap.
- The paper has no cost or latency numbers beyond the re-planning round counts.

BUILDS ON
Retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020); DEPS interactive planning (Wang et al., 2023b); self-debug (Chen et al., 2023); Reflexion-style self-explain (Shinn et al., 2023); Inner Monologue (Huang et al., 2022b); ReAct (Yao et al., 2022); Voyager (Wang et al., 2023a); Ghost in the Minecraft (Zhu et al., 2023, text memory); Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023, explicit memory); MineCLIP (Fan et al., 2022); VPT (Baker et al., 2022); STEVE-1 (Lifshitz et al., 2023, the controller); self-instruct (Wang et al., 2022); Minecraft Universe Benchmark (Lin et al., 2023a).

CODE
Memory record (App A.3, p.23): "memory is a list where each trajectory experience is encoded as a dictionary, including the keys task, state, and plan."
Retrieval-augmented planning (Eq. 1, p.7): p(y|x) ≈ sum over z in top-k of p_η(z|x) · p_θ(y|x,z)
Ranking (Eq. 2, p.8): p_η(z|x) ∝ CLIP_v(s_z)ᵀ CLIP_v(s_x)
Query-gen prompt (Fig 5, p.8): "My current task is <task>, but I have never accomplished this task before. What related tasks might be helpful for me to complete <task>?"
Planning prompt format (App A.2, Prompt 1, p.21): plans are Python-like code (mine(obj=..., tool=...), craft(obj=..., materials=..., tool=...)). The self-check prompt (Prompt 4) walks inventory state step by step.

FIGURES
- Fig 3 (p.5): architecture plus self-improving loop (query gen -> retrieve -> planner -> controller -> save to shared memory). Fastest explanation of the memory loop.
- Fig 5 (p.8): query generation via reasoning. Backward sub-goal search, then retrieval for those sub-goals present in memory.
- Fig 4 (p.6): self-check and self-explain flow.
- Fig 7 (p.13): success vs memory size. Shows the learning curve.
- Fig 8 (p.13): text vs text+reasoning vs multimodal+reasoning vs no memory. This is the ablation to read for numbers.
- Fig 9 (p.14): success vs game time against VPT-RL and curriculum variants.
- Fig 2 right (p.4): cross-task transfer heatmap.

PROBLEMS
- Figure-embedded numbers are scrambled in the extraction (Fig 1, 6, 7, 8, 9), so I did not quote them.
- Internal text inconsistencies: "Table 6" on p.12 means Fig 6; "graph on the right side of Figure 7" on p.14 means Fig 9; the abstract's "5 times" vs the body's "more than doubled"; Fig 1 caption "6% vs. 2.5%".
- The Table 2 extraction interleaves per-task rows with group averages. I used only the clearly labelled AVG values and the text.
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF.
